transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Nice to meet you, Doctor. Well, honestly, I made this appointment because things at work have just gotten completely out of hand, and I don't really know what else to do at this point. I'm a computer support specialist—I actually have a graduate degree, so I'm very used to dealing with complex, high-level systems, and I've been doing this for a long time. But lately... well, what brings me in is that I just can't keep my mind on a task long enough to actually finish it anymore. 

And the worst part is, it happens even when it's incredibly important. It's so frustrating because I know exactly what I'm *supposed* to be doing, but my brain just refuses to cooperate. Like, for example, I'll get an urgent ticket for a client's network problem. A server goes down, or there's some weird routing issue, and I'll pull up the diagnostic logs to start tracing the root cause. I'll sit down, totally intending to just knock it out, and then... I don't know, ten minutes later, I'll suddenly snap to and realize I've literally just reread the exact same block of log entries three or four times. I'm just staring at the text, reading the lines over and over, but I still don't know what they actually say. Nothing is sticking. And it's just... it's really starting to scare me, because if I can't even read a basic log file without my mind just totally detaching and wandering off, how am I supposed to fix these networks? It just takes me forever to get through the simplest things now.
When did you first start noticing this difficulty concentrating? Was it something that came on suddenly, or has it been building up gradually over weeks or months?

Well, you know, it’s... it’s an interesting question, because it didn’t just pop up out of thin air like a light switch flipping, but the really severe part—the part where it’s actually destroying my ability to function and taking me forever to do anything—that started very specifically about a year and ten months ago. 

I know the exact timeframe because... well, that’s when I was fired from my previous job. And that was just a massive, massive upheaval for me. I had been there a long time, I knew the environment perfectly, and over the years, I had built up all these highly specific, intricate systems just to keep myself on track. I mean, I had a whole workflow. I used multiple monitors arranged in a certain way, I had physical whiteboards color-coded for different priority levels, I had automated scripts that would literally ping me if a ticket sat too long... all these rigid, external structures that I didn’t even fully realize were basically holding my professional life together. 

Then the firing happened—which, honestly, was a whole nightmare of corporate restructuring that I still don't completely agree with, they just came in and completely gutted the senior IT staff—and I lost all of it. I lost the office, the routine, the systems. And ever since that happened, for the last year and ten months, it’s just been a total freefall. Without those guardrails I had set up, my brain just... it just scatters. I sit down at my new desk and there's nothing forcing me to stay on the path. So I guess you could say the underlying issue might have been lurking there in the background, but the serious trouble, the absolute inability to concentrate on a simple log file, hit me like a freight train the second I lost the systems that were keeping me anchored.

Besides the trouble concentrating, how has your mood been over this past year and ten months? Have you been feeling persistently sad, empty, or anxious, or has your mood been relatively normal aside from the frustration about work?

Well, sad or empty? No, I wouldn't use those words at all. I don't feel empty. If anything, I feel very full, but full of aggravation, you know? It’s really just the frustration, but when I say frustration, I need to be clear—it is this deep, pervasive, almost physical irritation with myself that just builds and builds as the day goes on. 

Because, you see, I know I'm a smart guy. I have the degree, I have decades of experience in this field. So when I sit there and my brain is just... buffering, for lack of a better term, I don't feel sad, I just feel incredibly annoyed. Not anxiety, either—it's not like I'm sitting there panicking or worrying about the future or my health or anything like that. It’s just this sheer, unadulterated annoyance that I can't just *do* the thing I sat down to do. 

Like, just last Tuesday, I was trying to map out a simple subnet for a small office client. It’s something I could have done in my sleep ten years ago. And I just sat there at my desk, and I kept getting up to get coffee, and then I'd look back at the screen, and I just felt this intense tension—just this absolute anger at my own brain because the knowledge is right there in my head, but the bridge to actually executing it is just totally washed out. My wife even mentions it. She says I come home and I'm just wound up, grumbling about how I wasted the whole day staring at a wall. 

But it's definitely not sadness. I still enjoy my life outside of this mess, I still love my family, I still care about things. It's just this massive, looming cloud of 'why can't I just function like a normal professional anymore?' that hangs over my head Monday through Friday. So, no, not depressed or anxious... just profoundly, exhaustingly frustrated with myself.

Before you were fired from your previous job—going back to your childhood, school years, and early career—did you ever struggle with staying focused on tasks, or did you always find it relatively easy to concentrate back then?

Well, you know, it’s funny you ask that, because... well, I guess the short answer is yes, I did struggle, but it looked different back then. I mean, my mother—she actually still jokes about this, even now that I'm in my fifties—she loves to bring up my old report cards from grade school. It’s sort of a family legend at this point. 

She kept them all in this old shoebox, and she'd pull them out, and it was always the same story, year after year. The teachers would always write, you know, "He’s a very bright boy, very intelligent," but then there was always this massive "but" attached to it. It was always, "but he never stays in his seat." I was apparently always getting up, walking around the classroom, looking out the window, bothering the kid next to me. And they always complained that I blurted out answers. Like, the teacher would ask a question, and before she even finished the sentence, I’d just shout out the answer without raising my hand. I just couldn't hold it in, it was like the thought hit my brain and bypassed my mouth entirely. 

And the homework! Oh man, the homework was a whole other disaster. My mom still laughs about how I would actually sit down at the kitchen table, do the entire math worksheet, put it in my folder, and then somehow, between the kitchen table and the teacher's desk the next morning, it would just vanish. I lost my homework all the time, even when I had actually done it. It drove my parents crazy. 

So, yeah, the trouble was definitely there, but back then, I guess it was more physical? More bouncing off the walls and losing pieces of paper. As I got older and went through high school and grad school, I sort of figured out how to sit still—mostly—and I developed those systems I told you about to keep track of my work. But looking back, I guess that same restless, scattered energy was always there, I just learned how to build a fortress around it so I could get my degrees and do my job. Until the fortress fell down, obviously.

Over this past year and ten months since you were fired, or even going back further, have you ever had periods where you felt unusually energetic, needed less sleep than normal, or felt like you could do way more than you typically can—where your mind was racing with ideas or plans?

Energetic? No, no, definitely not. Honestly, I wish I had a period where I felt unusually energetic, because maybe then I could actually get something done! But no, if anything, I feel like I'm constantly running on empty lately, mostly just from the sheer mental toll of trying to force myself to focus all day. It’s exhausting. 

And as for the sleep thing... I've always been someone who absolutely requires a solid, uninterrupted seven to eight hours. Even way back in grad school, you know, when all the other guys in the computer lab were pulling these crazy all-nighters, chugging energy drinks and writing code until dawn, I just couldn't do it. My brain would completely shut down by 2 AM. And it's the exact same story now. I usually go to bed around 11:30, I wake up at 7:00, and I never, ever have those nights where I feel like I just don't need sleep. If I get less than seven hours, the next day is a complete write-off. I mean, even more of a write-off than it already is these days. 

And when you ask about my mind racing with ideas and plans... see, I need to make a distinction there. My mind races, sure, but absolutely not with *plans*. It's not like I'm suddenly hit with a grand vision for a new software startup or some brilliant new server architecture, and I'm just bursting with this incredible drive to build it. No, my mind races with... well, junk. Just absolute static. 

It’s racing with things like, "Oh, I need to check that email," or "Wait, did I remember to renew the SSL certificate on my personal domain?", or "I wonder why they deprecated that one specific API in the last update, I should go read the patch notes from three years ago." It’s a very unproductive, scattered kind of racing. It’s not energetic, and it's certainly not me feeling like I can take on the world. It’s just noisy. So no, no periods of feeling like Superman or not needing sleep or anything like that. Just the same old frustrating, exhausting daily grind where I'm trying to sift through the noise.

When you were in your twenties and thirties, before you were fired—during those years when you had your job and your systems in place—did you still struggle with staying focused and organized, or had those childhood problems pretty much gone away by then?

Well, it’s... it’s a bit of a complicated answer, honestly. Did the problems go away? No, not entirely. But they weren't causing this kind of catastrophic failure, if you see what I mean. 

Back in my twenties and thirties, I was deeply embedded in the corporate IT world. And the thing about corporate IT is that they build the structure for you. Everything is a ticket. You get a ticket, it has a priority level, it has a deadline, you fix the server issue, you close the ticket. Plus, I had an office to go to, I had a manager who needed weekly reports, I had... well, I had scaffolding. 

So, internally? Sure, my brain was still doing its thing. My desk was always a complete disaster zone of tangled ethernet cables and sticky notes, and I always needed, like, three monitors going at once just to keep all my active windows visible so I wouldn't forget they existed. But I managed. I made it work because the environment forced me to. 

The actual *serious* trouble—the complete inability to function that brought me in here to talk to you—that really only started about a year and ten months ago. Exactly a year and ten months, actually, because that's when I was fired. And when I lost that job, I lost all of those external systems that used to keep me on track. The scaffolding just vanished overnight. 

Suddenly, it’s just me, sitting in my home office, trying to do freelance consulting, and there's no automated ticketing system, no boss checking in, no rigid nine-to-five schedule. Just me and my own brain. And without those external pressures forcing me to stay organized, I just... I can't do it. I’ve tried setting up my own task boards, you know, color-coded and everything, spending hours tweaking the software, but it doesn't work because I know I'm the one who made the rules, so I can just ignore them. 

So, yeah, the underlying stuff was probably always there, buzzing in the background, but the really severe problems, this total breakdown in my ability to work and stay focused? That’s strictly been the last year and ten months, ever since that corporate structure was pulled out from under me.

When you were working at that previous job for all those years—before you were fired—did you find that you needed those external systems and structures to stay organized, or would you have been able to manage your work and keep track of things just fine even without them?

Oh, I absolutely needed them. There is zero chance I would have managed without them. I mean, I know this for a fact because I can see exactly what my life looks like right now without them, and it is not pretty. 

You see, at the old job, the environment basically did the executive functioning for me. But now? Without that old ticketing system we used, and without the escalation calendar—which, by the way, was this incredibly useful tool that automatically flagged when a client issue was nearing its service level agreement deadline—without those specific things, my days just completely dissolve. 

They turn into these... these massive, unmanageable piles of sticky notes everywhere. My desk, my monitor, the wall next to my desk, it's just covered in them. And it’s not even just work stuff, it’s a complete jumble. It's half-finished emails sitting open in my drafts folder because I got distracted trying to find an attachment, mixed in with reminders for the local chess club, mixed in with actual, critical parts orders for clients... like, I'll have a note about ordering a new RAID controller right next to a note about the chess club tournament schedule. 

And the real problem, the thing that just paralyzes me, is that when I look at that pile, I honestly can't tell what has to happen first. Without the ticketing system assigning a priority level to everything, my brain just looks at the chess club reminder and the server parts order and treats them like they have the exact same level of urgency. I can't sequence the tasks. I just stare at the mess, trying to figure out where to start, and I usually can't figure it out until something is already overdue and blowing up in my face. Someone will call me asking where their hardware is, and that's the only way I know, "Ah, okay, that was the priority." So, to answer your question, yes, I desperately needed that external structure. Without it, I'm just drowning in paper and missed deadlines, just completely unable to sort the data on my own.

Going back to your twenties and thirties at that previous job—before you were fired—when you were using those external systems like the ticketing software and the escalation calendar, did you feel like you *needed* those tools to keep yourself organized, or could you have managed your work and kept track of priorities reasonably well even without them if you had to?

Right, yeah, I mean—like I was just touching on a second ago, it’s exactly that. I absolutely *had* to have them. Even back then in my twenties and thirties, if you had stripped away that ticketing software or that escalation calendar, I would have crashed and burned just as hard as I am right now. It wouldn't have mattered that I was younger or anything like that. 

Because without those specific tools doing the heavy lifting for my brain, my days just... they completely unravel. They turn into these exact same piles of sticky notes I'm dealing with today. Just endless, chaotic piles everywhere. Half-finished emails sitting open on my screens, reminders for the chess club buried under actual, critical parts orders for clients... it’s all just one big blur of information. 

And the terrifying part—the part that hasn't changed no matter how old I am—is that I honestly can't tell what has to happen first. I can stare at a note about ordering a replacement server part and a note about a chess tournament, and my brain just refuses to rank them. It's all just noise. I literally can't see the priority until something is already overdue, you know? Until the deadline has blown past, the system is down, and someone is calling me furious because I dropped the ball. So, yes, even back then, if I had to manage my own priorities without the software telling me what was red-alert urgent? No chance. Zero. I would have been just as paralyzed by the piles of notes then as I am today.

Outside of work—things like hobbies, personal projects, managing your household, or things you do with your family—are you able to start and finish those tasks without the same kind of struggle you're having with work, or do you find yourself getting stuck and unable to focus on those things too?

Well, outside of work... you know, it’s funny you ask that, because it’s something I’ve tried to think about, but to be completely honest with you, I really don't know. I just don't have a clear answer for you on that. 

It’s hard to say if it’s the exact same kind of struggle, because the context is just so entirely different, isn't it? I mean, with the house, there’s no ticketing system for, say, fixing the gutter or organizing the garage, so I don't really have a metric to measure my progress against, if that makes sense. I guess I haven't really noticed if I get stuck in the exact same way, because... well, if a personal project doesn't get finished, nobody is calling me screaming about server downtime. 

Take the chess club I was talking about earlier. I have all those sticky notes for it mixed in with everything else, but if I don't go, I just don't go. Is that me getting stuck? Is that me being unable to focus and finish a task? Or is that just me not going because I'm overwhelmed by the work stuff? I really couldn't tell you. It's all just sort of bleeding together right now. 

So trying to parse out whether my personal life is stalling out in the exact same mechanical way my professional life is... I just don't have the data to give you a solid answer. I’ve been so completely consumed by the fact that my freelance consulting is a total disaster that I haven't really stopped to analyze how I'm handling my hobbies or family time. I'm just not sure how to evaluate it, honestly.

When you sit down to do something you actually enjoy—like playing chess, or working on a personal hobby that interests you—do you find yourself able to focus and stay engaged with it, or do you experience that same scattered, wandering attention that you get with work tasks?

Well, with chess... you know, I try to sit down and study a match, maybe look at some classic games, which I've loved doing for years. But honestly, it all just circles back to the main issue, the whole reason I'm sitting here talking to you today. What really brings me in, the thing that finally made me realize I needed help, is that I just cannot keep my mind on a task long enough to finish it anymore. Period. It doesn't matter what it is, but it's especially bad when it's work—even when it's incredibly important and a client's entire infrastructure is hanging in the balance. 

Like, just the other day, I was trying to trace a client's network problem. A pretty standard routing issue, something I've done a thousand times. I sit down at my desk, I pull up the diagnostic logs, and I'm looking at the screen... and ten minutes will go by. Ten whole minutes of me supposedly working. And I'll suddenly snap to and realize, with this awful sinking feeling in my stomach, that I have just reread the exact same block of log entries three times, maybe more, and I still have absolutely no idea what they say. 

It's like the words are just shapes on the monitor. My eyes are physically moving over the text, I'm scrolling down the terminal window, but my brain is completely somewhere else. I'm trying to force myself to process the error codes, and the information just slides right off my brain. I'll read a line, get to the end of it, and realize I didn't retain a single syllable. And it's terrifying, frankly. Because when you're a support specialist, you have to be able to parse that data. You can't just glaze over. But I just sit there, staring at the logs, trying to grab onto the thread of the problem, and it just evaporates. So whether it's analyzing a chess board or a command prompt, the focus just isn't there. I can't sustain it at all, and I just end up reading the same line over and over and getting absolutely nothing out of it.

When you sit down to play chess—not studying games, but actually playing a game against someone or against a computer—can you stay focused on the board and the moves, or do you find your attention drifting away the same way it does with work?

Actually playing a game... right. Well, see, that's the thing. I wish I could give you a definitive yes or no on that, but... I honestly just don't know. I really couldn't say. 

Because if I try to really think about it—say I log into my chess account online, which I've had for probably fifteen years at this point, or even if I were to pull out the physical board in the living room... when I'm sitting there making moves, I'm not really running a diagnostic on my own brain, you know? Like, am I staring at the knight because I'm actively calculating four moves deep, or am I staring at the knight because my brain has completely checked out and I'm secretly stressing about a client's firewall configuration? I honestly couldn't tell you the difference anymore. 

And as for playing against an actual human being across the table, I haven't actually made it down to the club in so long—mostly because of all the scheduling chaos and those endless piles of sticky notes I was telling you about—that I just don't have a recent example to draw from. I'll sit down at the computer to play a quick bot match just to try and decompress, but I don't track my own attention span while I'm doing it. I might be zoning out between moves, I might be totally locked in, but I just... I haven't paid enough attention to my own attention to give you a straight answer. 

So, as much as I'd like to say, 'Oh sure, when I play a game, my mind is sharp as a tack,' or even tell you that it's exactly as broken as my work focus, I just don't have a clear picture of it. I haven't really noticed one way or the other, because the background stress of my consulting business falling apart is just so incredibly loud, even when I'm supposedly doing something I enjoy.

Let me ask this more directly: when you're doing something that you find genuinely engaging and interesting—something that really captures your attention naturally, like watching a movie you love or having a conversation with someone you care about—do you find that your attention stays with it, or do you experience that same scattered, wandering feeling you described with the work tasks?

I hear what you're asking, I really do. You're trying to figure out if it happens with a movie or a good conversation, something that's supposed to be naturally engaging. But... look, I know I keep circling back to the work thing, and I'm probably sounding like a completely broken record at this point, but I just can't separate it out right now. 

Because what brings me in here—the entire reason I finally picked up the phone and made this appointment—is that I simply cannot keep my mind on a task long enough to finish it anymore. Period. And the fact that it happens even when it is critically, financially important is what's absolutely destroying me. 

Like I was saying before about that network problem. I'll sit down to trace a routing issue for a client—something I absolutely have to do, something their entire business infrastructure depends on—and ten minutes will go by, and I'll realize I've just reread the exact same block of log entries three times over. And I still won't know what they say! It's like my brain just refuses to hold onto the information, no matter how high the stakes are. 

So, whether I'm watching a movie or talking to a friend... maybe I'm scattered then, too, I honestly don't know. I probably am. But it’s so hard to even care about whether I can pay attention to a movie when I can't even focus on the things that are keeping a roof over my head. That's the part that I just can't get past. When you can't even force yourself to read a few lines of text to save your own business, it just completely overshadows everything else.

If you're sitting down to watch a TV show or movie that you really enjoy, can you typically watch the whole thing without your mind wandering away, or do you find yourself getting distracted and losing track of what's happening on screen?

Look, I... I really don't know. I know you're trying to get a read on how I handle leisure time, like putting on a movie or a TV show, but I just don't have a clear answer for you on that. 

If I sit down on the couch in the evening, you know, grab the remote, and put on some sci-fi movie or a new series on Netflix—something I supposedly enjoy—I'm not sitting there taking notes on my own mental state. I might be watching every single frame and following the plot perfectly, or I might be completely checked out, just staring at the glow of the television while my brain is a million miles away. I honestly couldn't tell you which it is. I just haven't noticed. 

You have to understand, I'm not evaluating my movie-watching skills because... well, because it just doesn't matter to me right now. I don't care if I miss a plot point in a TV show. It's just not on my radar. What I care about, the thing that is consuming every waking second of my life right now, is that I can't read three lines of a diagnostic log without my brain completely wiping the slate clean. That's the crisis. That's the thing that's threatening my livelihood. 

So when it comes to movies, or TV, or whatever else... I just don't know. I don't track it. I couldn't tell you if I'm distracted or if I'm glued to the screen, because it's all just background noise compared to the fact that I can't do my actual job.

When you're having a conversation with your wife or a friend—just talking back and forth—do you find that you can follow what they're saying and stay engaged in the conversation, or do you notice your mind drifting away during those interactions?

Doctor, I... I know you're trying to get a complete picture here, asking about my wife and my friends, and I appreciate that, I really do. But I feel like I'm just going to frustrate you because I have to go back to what I was saying before. I know I keep repeating myself, and I apologize for being so fixated on this one thing, but it's just... it's the entire reason I'm here. 

What actually brought me into this office, the thing that finally made me seek help, isn't about whether I'm a good listener at dinner. It's the fact that I absolutely cannot keep my mind on a task long enough to finish it anymore. That's the whole crisis. Even when it's something critically important! Like I was trying to explain earlier with that client's network problem... I'll be sitting there at my desk, trying to trace a routing issue, knowing perfectly well that their business operations are practically halted until I fix it. The stakes are high. And then ten minutes will just vanish. I'll snap back to reality and realize I've just sat there and reread the exact same sequence of log entries three times over. Three times! And I still don't have the faintest clue what they actually say. My brain just won't hold the data, no matter how hard I try to force it. 

So, conversations? Talking with my wife or a buddy? Maybe I drift off when she's talking, maybe I don't. I'm sure she'd have an opinion on it if you asked her. But I'm in such a state of constant, overwhelming panic over the fact that I can't even read a basic server log to keep my consulting business afloat, that I just can't give you a good answer about my social interactions. I can't evaluate my engagement in a chat about the weekend when the inability to complete my actual work is just eclipsing everything else in my life right now.

I understand work is consuming your thoughts right now. But let me ask you this directly: when you're driving your car, can you focus on the road and the driving task without your mind wandering, or do you find yourself getting distracted and losing track of where you are?

Doc, I hear you. Driving. You want to know if I zone out behind the wheel. And... look, maybe I do. Maybe I missed a turn on the way to your office today, I honestly couldn't even tell you. But I know I am frustrating you, and I know I am completely stonewalling your questions, but you have to understand why I just can't focus on evaluating my driving, or movies, or dinner chats right now. My entire career is literally crumbling in front of my eyes. 

The absolute only reason I am sitting in this chair today is because I have completely lost the ability to keep my mind on a task long enough to actually finish it. It just doesn't happen anymore. It doesn't matter how critical it is or how much pressure I'm under. I've got these clients, right? They rely on me to keep their infrastructure running. And I'll sit down at my desk to trace a routing problem—something that is entirely holding up their business operations, something I've done a thousand times before. I pull up the diagnostic logs, I put my cursor on the screen, and I try to read. 

And then... I don't know, time just evaporates. Ten, fifteen minutes will go by, and I'll snap out of whatever fog I'm in and realize I have just read the exact same block of log entries three times in a row. Three times! And I'll look at the screen, panic setting in, and realize I still have absolutely no idea what they say. The information just will not stay in my head, no matter how hard I try to grip it. 

So... driving? I don't know. I'm probably just on autopilot. But I can't even bring myself to care about my commute when I can't even finish a basic diagnostic task to save my own business. That's the fire I need to put out.

When you were at your previous job, before you were fired—back when you had all those systems in place and everything was running smoothly—did you ever have moments where you just couldn't focus, even on things that weren't work-related, or was the scattered attention something that only showed up when you didn't have those external structures to rely on?

You know, it's... it's interesting you phrase it that way, about the external structures. Because when I look back at my old job, the one I had before the bottom fell out... I really didn't have this problem. Or, if I did, it certainly wasn't ruining my life like it is now, and I definitely wasn't noticing it spilling over into the rest of my life. 

Back then, I had everything so completely dialed in. I mean, I had automated ticketing systems, calendar alerts, project managers checking in, daily stand-up meetings... a whole environment built around me that just forced me to stay on the rails. The environment did the heavy lifting for my attention. If my mind even tried to wander, there was a system in place to immediately pull me back. I was highly functioning. I was a professional. 

But then I was fired. And that was... let's see, it's been about a year and ten months now. One year and ten months of just absolute, unmitigated chaos. 

Because the day they let me go, they didn't just take my paycheck. They took the entire scaffolding of my life. All those systems, all those external structures that told me where to look and what to do next—just wiped out overnight. And ever since that exact point, for the last twenty-two months, it's been this relentless downward spiral. This serious, catastrophic trouble with my focus... it really only showed up after I lost that job and lost the systems that used to keep me on track. 

Now, I'm out here trying to run my own consulting business, and there's no boss, there's no automated system forcing my hand, there's no one looking over my shoulder. It's just me and a blank screen. And without all those external guardrails I used to rely on, my brain just completely scatters. So, no, it wasn't like this before. It's been exactly a year and ten months of this nightmare, ever since that structure was ripped away from me.

Before you were fired from that job—let's say when you were 25 or 30 years old, back when you had all those systems in place and everything was working well—if you had tried to sit down and read something difficult without any external structure forcing you to pay attention, like reading a technical manual on your own time at home with no deadline, do you think you would have been able to focus and get through it, or would you have had that same problem where your mind just wouldn't stick with it?

You know, it's funny you specifically bring up reading a technical manual on my own time, because people always assume that if you're in IT, you just love sitting around reading documentation in your free time. But honestly? Even back then in my twenties and thirties, and definitely now... quiet things just don't work for me. They really never have. 

You're talking about doing something without a deadline, just sitting peacefully. But quiet things that should relax me—whether it's trying to read a manual just to learn something new, or sitting through a movie with my wife on a Friday night, or even trying one of those breathing exercises she's always suggesting I do to manage my stress—it's a disaster. It's supposed to be relaxing, right? But I sit there, and it lasts maybe... I don't know, a few minutes? A few minutes, tops. 

And then I'm just crawling out of my skin. I start muttering comments under my breath about whatever is on the TV or the page, or I'm pulling out my phone to check something completely unrelated, or I just end up physically getting up from the couch or the desk for absolutely no real reason. I'll tell my wife I just need a glass of water, or I'll go check the thermostat, but really, my brain is just screaming at me to move, to do something else. 

So, to answer your question about being 25 or 30 and reading a manual without a boss breathing down my neck or a system in place... no. No, I couldn't just sit and focus on it. While the patient attributes recent severe functional impairment to job loss 22 months ago, the underlying neurodevelopmental disorder has been present since childhood. The loss of external structure unmasked and exacerbated pre-existing ADHD symptoms rather than causing them de novo.
